catalog_quote: 1.3 Tones Deiga is a tone language, with lexical and grammatical tone . There are two tonemes, a high one and a low one . Contour tones are rare and have to be analysed as complex tones, consisting of a high and a low tone, e.g. éɛbáày (ἑεbágì) ' they are being beaten ' . Compare the following minimal pairs: (i) lexical tone: ἐνὲ name à be.ID difè ἑνέ roots á be.LC difé kisra dough to stay (ii) grammatical tone: isò - mí sHe ran isò - mí sHe runs àblà - mí sHe danced àblá - mí sHe dances . All data are fully marked for tone but may not be very reliable in this respect . I suspect that a number of tones recorded as low are in fact down - stepped high tones before a new constituent . Furthermore, there seem to be certain tone rules across boundaries which I have not been able to clarify . 2 The verb [Reh 1994: 201, chained Google Books; scan shows IPA as Greek letters] ... Hall & Hall 2004: 65 (open text): The tone system has not been fully analysed for any of the Kadugli-Krongo languages. ... The other Kadugli-Krongo languages that we have studied also have two tones, with a considerable amount of pitch conditioning. ... Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 19 sec. 2 (snippets, group-level after Stevenson): 2a. Stevenson states that tone is less important than stress, but tonal doublets have been found in some languages ... Tone and Stress, however, are not marked in the following sections.

Stevenson states that tone is less important than stress, but tonal doublets have been found in some languages: nya hill nya wind; 'ofo to vomit 'ofo mound 2b. new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Kadugli-Krongo group as a whole (Katcha-based, Krongo examples), dynamic stress is said to matter more than tone and to interact with tone and consonant length; no statement of where stress falls, and nothing specific to Keiga.
new_statements.exceptions: None; examples show stress on either first or second syllable in Krongo ('korugut vs ku'rigit) tied to tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level survey remark (Kadugli-Krongo family), second-hand from Stevenson; reconstructed from scanned snippets with diacritics lost; word-level citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The only statement recovered is group-level for Kadugli-Krongo (Tucker & Bryan's chapter is Katcha-based with Krongo examples; Keiga appears only in the dialect list 'Western: TULISHI, KEIGA, KANGA'). Blench 2005 and Hall & Hall 2004 treat Keiga proper (Kayigang; dialect clusters Ambong, Lubung, Tumuro) = keig1242. Reh 1994 'Deiga' = Keiga (keig1242).

new_statements.quote: All Kadu languages are almost certainly tone languages. I have more or less uncritically assumed a two tone system, and I have occasionally heard and marked downstep. Falling tones are rare, and rising tones even more so. Reh, too, describes Krongo and Yegang as having two-tone Systems, and she points out cases where tone distinguishes lexical items as well as different grammatical forms of the same item. [...] The tonal variations, both within and across languages, are indicative of interesting tonal processes, but the data are insufficient to analyse thé various tonal Systems. [p. 19:] High tone is marked with an acute accent; low tone is unmarked.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Deiga has an empty rule and the one existing statement (Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. 19 sec. 2, after Stevenson) is read 'tone language, no stress statement'. Schadeberg 1994 gives the same picture: tonal (two tones plus downstep, citing Reh's Yegang sketch) and silent on stress. It does not repeat Stevenson's remark that stress matters more than tone, but it does not contradict it either. Identity: his '2. Yegang' = Stevenson's 'Keiga', data from the dialect of Keiga Tummero (Timero), informant Tayyib Abd el-Baagi (p. 12), i.e. keig1242.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Keiga/Yegang and the other Kadu languages are treated as two-tone languages (high vs. low, occasional downstep); the article contains no statement on word stress, accent or prominence at all (the words 'stress' and 'prominence' do not occur; 'accent' occurs only as the name of the acute diacritic for high tone). Wordlist forms carry tone marks only.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement to except from); the author flags that his tone marking is 'more or less uncritical' and that the data are insufficient to analyse the tonal systems
new_statements.identity_note: Schadeberg's list 2 'Yegang' is explicitly equated with Stevenson's 'Keiga' and recorded from the dialect of Keiga Tummero (Timero), locality dl ma-yegaq (Reh: k-eegaq), language sani ma-yegaq (Reh: d-ayga), i.e. the Deiga/Keiga of Reh 1994 = keig1242, not Keiga Jirru (a Nyimang variety).

tone_statements.quote: 4.3.6 Tones in Keiga Language: Schadeberg (1994) and Reh (1984) assume two tones for some Kadugli languages (Kanga and Kadugli). On the other hand, Matsushita (1984) posits three for Kadugli, the most common system, though it appears to be two tones plus down step, which is also common in many Kadugli- Krongo languages in the region. As one of the Kadugli languages Keiga has two tones (high and low).
